**Status:** Evidence-backed investigation; recommendation proposed, not adopted or
implemented.

**Verified against:** `jheem_analyses@426f03d125ab8a2a24c9b2b3230fbf4304894761`,
`jheem2@90b68ad500c12bdfe8f9dc6616e9a846fb4ae3d1`, and
`bayesian.simulations@4e0d13e85857396bb0e6e2ac1d244775b2145f75`.
Production-cache measurements were taken read-only from the shared calibration
store on 2026-09-02.

**Operational clarification (2026-08-26):** Routine calibrations run on the
team's shared servers. Rockfish support exists in the source tree, but it is not
the normal execution target. The requested feature is periodic evaluation of
mixing while MCMC is running, followed by an explainable early stop when a
configured number of parameters exceed a threshold. The initial design discussion
was exploratory; the diagnostic, thresholds, cadence, and stop semantics remain to
be specified.

## Assessment

The existing cache is sufficient for a useful first observability feature, but it
is not itself a job-monitoring or online-diagnostic contract.

A completed checkpoint exposes per-chain progress, cumulative acceptance, runtime,
current parameter state, and—in post-burn chunk files—parameter samples and total
log likelihoods. That can support a low-I/O status report immediately and richer
diagnostics later. It cannot establish whether a process is currently running,
queued, sleeping between retries, or dead. It also publishes mutable control files
with direct `save()` calls, so a concurrent reader must expect transient load
failures.

The operational clarification changes the target, but not the package boundary.
A defensive, read-only cache snapshot in `bayesian.simulations` remains the
foundation. The first operator-valued vertical slice should now pair that snapshot
with one explicitly defined mixing policy and a graceful stop request evaluated at
completed checkpoint boundaries. The policy and operator-facing report belong in
`jheem_analyses`; generic cache publication, hook invocation, and stop mechanics
belong in `bayesian.simulations`.

Production measurements rule out repeatedly loading science chunks as the online
diagnostic transport. A recent SHIELD checkpoint serialized 44.2 MB to retain ten
draws for 174 parameters; the parameter, likelihood, and acceptance payload needed
by a diagnostic serialized to 5.0 KB. The sampler already holds that payload in
memory before clearing the completed chunk. It should publish a small atomic
diagnostic sidecar at that point, while the full chunk remains the scientific
record.

An unrestricted callback inside the per-iteration loop is not yet a sound design.
The current server workflows commonly run chains independently, and each worker
holds only its own in-progress draws. A multi-chain diagnostic requires a common
published prefix across chains. Checkpoint boundaries already provide that durable
exchange point and limit a stop to a resumable state. Sub-checkpoint evaluation
would require explicit partial-checkpoint and recovery semantics.

## What was traced

The standard calibration path is:

1. An application specification and calibration registry are sourced from
   `jheem_analyses`.
2. `jheem2::set.up.calibration()` builds the JHEEM engine, likelihood, adaptive
   Metropolis control, initial states, and cache
   (`jheem2:R/CALIBRATION_main.R:13-653`).
3. Setup creates one cache per
   `root/mcmc_runs/<version>/<location>/<calibration-code>` and one mutable control
   file per chain (`jheem2:R/FILE_MANAGER_file_manager.R:381-391`).
4. `jheem2::run.calibration()` delegates selected chains to
   `bayesian.simulations::run.mcmc.from.cache()` and attempts to cache a summary
   after the run (`jheem2:R/CALIBRATION_main.R:715-775`).
5. Each chain runs independently in cache-sized chunks. At a chunk boundary the
   sampler writes a post-burn MCMC chunk, updates its in-memory chain state, marks
   the chunk done, and overwrites the chain-control file
   (`bayesian.simulations:R/cache.R:350-419`).
6. Assembly reads completed chunks into an MCMC or JHEEM simulation set; application
   scripts save the resulting simset separately.

Routine operation uses the shared JHU servers. The checked-in server-oriented EHE
and SHIELD runners commonly invoke one selected chain at a time. The package can
also run selected chains in parallel, but `parallel.lapply()` gives each worker an
independent process and memory space (`bayesian.simulations:R/parallelization.R:3-58`).
Therefore no chain-local callback can inspect the live, uncommitted state of its
siblings.

For the alternative Rockfish path, `jheem_analyses` generates distinct setup,
per-location/per-chain run, and assembly jobs. The batch scripts write scheduler
output files, but the cache does not record Slurm job IDs or lifecycle state
(`jheem_analyses:cluster_scripts/batch_script_helpers.R:61-207`). SHIELD also has a
server-oriented modular runner that retries every caught run error up to 99 times,
describing each as a probable interrupted write and sleeping five minutes before
retrying (`jheem_analyses:applications/SHIELD/shield_calib_setup_and_run_modular.R:46-78`).
The cache alone cannot distinguish any of those states.

Ryan White parameter fitting is a second execution pattern, not a thin wrapper over
the standard cache. It runs short uncached MCMCs while transmuting an existing EHE
simset and publishes application-specific `rw_cache/chunk*.Rdata` files
(`jheem_analyses:applications/ryan_white/ryan_white_mcmc.R:221-386`). The proposed
first slice deliberately covers the standard EHE/SHIELD cache path; Ryan White
needs a separate adapter if it is in scope.

## The observed checkpoint contract

`bayesian.simulations` owns the serialized classes and file layout
(`R/cache.R:8-55`):

```text
<calibration-dir>/
└── cache/
    ├── global_control.Rdata
    ├── chain1_control.Rdata
    ├── chain2_control.Rdata
    ├── chain_1/
    │   ├── chain1_chunk<N>.Rdata
    │   └── ...
    └── chain_2/
        └── ...
```

The global control is created during setup and describes the sampler, chains,
chunk sizes, burn boundary, and chain-control filenames. It also serializes the
MCMC control, whose JHEEM simulation and likelihood closures can capture an engine
and data manager; its production size must not be assumed small. A chain control
is overwritten at each completed chunk and contains its chunk filenames plus:

- the cache and chain IDs;
- a `chunk.done` bitmap;
- cumulative accepted proposals and completed runtime;
- the resumable adaptive chain state;
- one seed per chunk in the current source tree. Older production caches use a
  pre-seed schema and do not contain this slot.

Post-burn chunk files contain an `mcmcsim` object with parameter samples, total log
likelihoods and log priors, acceptance counts, run times, and retained JHEEM
simulations (`bayesian.simulations:R/mcmc_class.R:36-60`). Chunks wholly before burn
are not retained, though their completion is recorded in the chain control.

### Publication and resume semantics

The write order provides a useful implicit commit marker:

1. run a complete chunk in memory;
2. save its retained MCMC, if any;
3. update and save the chain control with `chunk.done[chunk] = TRUE`.

A successfully loaded chain control that marks a retained chunk done therefore
refers to a chunk whose save call returned; a non-retained chunk records completed
computation without a chunk file. If computation fails before the control update,
a later run starts from the prior completed chunk. If a chunk file exists but the
control still says it is incomplete, the runner recomputes and overwrites it.

This supports resumption at chunk boundaries. It does not make concurrent reads
atomic: both chunk and control files are written directly to their final paths,
without a temporary-file-plus-rename publication step. Cache deletion or recreation
can also race a reader.

Those guarantees describe package-controlled writes, not the provenance of a
directory after manual copying or reuse. In one production EHE cache, a chain
control created on July 9 marked all 1,000 chunks complete with zero recorded
runtime and zero accepted proposals, while that chain's chunk files were dated
July 1–6. The other inspected chain shared the same global ID and recorded 121.9
hours and 34,021 accepted proposals. The format contains no chunk-level run ID to
explain or validate the discrepancy. An inspector must report such inconsistencies
rather than inferring that every completed chunk was generated by the current
global control.

### Existing observability

There are already three partial interfaces:

- `jheem2::get.calibration.progress()` loads every chain control and returns the
  fraction of chunks marked done (`CALIBRATION_main.R:787-841`). It has no retry,
  freshness, runtime, acceptance, or process state.
- `jheem2::percentage.cache.complete()` duplicates that calculation with a
  hard-coded relative root (`CALIBRATION_main.R:1955-1976`).
- `bayesian.simulations::cache.progress()` is exported but stops with “not
  implemented yet” (`R/run_interface.R:435-443`).

The support package already implements plots for samples, total likelihood, and
acceptance plus an R-hat calculation (`R/postprocessing.R`). It does not implement
effective sample size, and its R-hat is not the current split, rank-normalized
diagnostic by default. These functions require assembled post-burn chunks; they do
not expose the chain currently computing inside an unfinished chunk.

`jheem2` also exposes `simset$get.mcmc.mixing.statistic()` after assembly
(`JHEEM_simulation.R:2133-2189`). For one chain it returns the ratio of parameter
variance in the first and last quarters. For multiple chains it implements a
custom R-hat-like calculation. The multi-chain code uses the total simulation
count where a per-chain count is required and collapses the between-chain
calculation across parameters, so it must be checked against a reference
implementation before it is used to terminate runs. The single-chain variance
ratio may encode established team practice, but it is not interchangeable with
multi-chain R-hat or effective sample size. “Mixing statistic” must name a specific
calculation before a threshold has operational meaning.

## Interpreting the requested callback

The exploratory request can be stated as a policy contract:

1. After at least a configured number of retained post-burn draws, evaluate every
   configured number of checkpoints.
2. Present the evaluator with a plain parameter table: one retained draw per row,
   parameter names as columns, plus explicit chain and iteration columns.
3. Return a structured decision containing `continue` or `request_stop`, the
   diagnostic name and configuration, and the parameters that crossed the
   threshold.
4. Persist that decision separately from the scientific cache. A stop request is
   checked by every chain after publishing a checkpoint, so all chains stop at a
   resumable boundary.
5. Record early termination as its own state, not as successful completion or an
   unexplained failure. Incomplete assembly remains an explicit downstream choice.

This separates mechanism from policy. `bayesian.simulations` need not know what a
JHEEM parameter means, while an analysis can supply a calibrated policy without
embedding application rules in the sampler. The hook should accept and return a
narrow, validated structure rather than an unconstrained function with access to
the sampler's mutable internals. Hook failures, repeated decisions, concurrent
writers, and the scope of a stop—one chain, one location, or a larger run—must have
defined behavior.

The proposed direction is also a **poor-run termination policy**, not ordinary
convergence stopping. A high R-hat-like value at one checkpoint means the chains
have not demonstrated convergence; it does not establish that additional sampling
cannot help. If the objective is to abandon runs unlikely to recover, the policy
needs evidence appropriate to that claim—for example persistence across several
checks, lack of improvement, or a separately validated pathological-state rule.
By contrast, conventional early completion would stop when all required
diagnostics are good. These two policies should not share an ambiguous threshold.

## Operator questions and available evidence

| Operator question | Available now | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Was the cache set up? | Global and chain controls | Setup can race inspection or later be deleted |
| How far has each location/chain progressed? | Chain `chunk.done`; global `chunk.size` for exact iterations | Updates only at chunk boundaries; global control may be expensive to load |
| Is it still alive? | Last control mtime; scheduler/process and log state outside cache | A long active chunk and a dead job look identical in the cache |
| How long has it run; rough ETA? | Completed runtime and iterations | No timing until the first chunk completes; future chunks may differ |
| Is it accepting proposals? | Cumulative accepted count | Aggregate only; no live value inside the current chunk |
| What is the likelihood trajectory? | Total log likelihood in retained chunks | Only post-burn, thinned samples; requires loading potentially large chunks |
| Are chains mixing? | Parameter samples after multiple chains retain a common prefix | Full chunks bundle large simulations; frequent checks need parameter-only sidecars and a statistically defined diagnostic |
| Why did it fail? | Scheduler/process state and output logs | No structured failure record or exception in the cache |
| Can it resume? | Chain state; per-chunk seeds only in the newer schema | Resume is chunk-granular; old caches do not fix checkpoint seeds, and run identity and package/code refs are not recorded |

## Verification experiments

These experiments test the source-level contract; they are not production I/O
benchmarks.

### Synthetic cache

At `bayesian.simulations@4e0d13e`, a two-chain synthetic Metropolis cache used 50
iterations per chain, burn 10, thin 2, and cache frequency 10. Running only chain 1
produced an inspectable state of 5/5 chunks for chain 1 and 0/5 for chain 2.
Incomplete assembly of chain 1 returned 20 retained draws with parameter samples
and total log likelihoods. This verifies that a status-only reader can avoid chunk
loads, while a later diagnostics reader can use published post-burn chunks.

### Concurrent direct-save read

The cache overwrites R serialization files using direct `save()`. In a stress test
that repeatedly overwrote an uncompressed 16 MB R object while another process
attempted 1,000 loads, 31 reads failed and 969 succeeded. The failure fraction is
specific to that test and must not be projected onto production. The result
establishes the failure mode: a read-only observer can encounter a partially
written serialization and must treat it as transient rather than cache corruption.

### Seed propagation

The current API accepts a `seed`, but `create.mcmc.cache()` does not pass it to
`do.create.cache()`, and `do.create.chain.cache.controls()` generates chunk seeds
without first applying the supplied value (`R/run_interface.R:181-218`,
`R/cache.R:184-262`). Two synthetic caches created in one process with the same
`seed = 123` stored different chunk-seed vectors. The cache remains repeatable when
resumed because it stores the generated per-chunk seeds, but the public seed does
not currently reproduce cache creation. A run manifest must not claim seed-level
reproducibility until this is fixed and regression-tested.

### Production caches

Two completed caches on the shared calibration store were inspected read-only on
2026-09-02. These measurements establish scale and schema variation; they do not
substitute for observing a live write from a server process.

| Measurement | Recent SHIELD cache | EHE state cache |
|---|---:|---:|
| Chains | 4 | 4 |
| Parameters | 174 | 382 |
| Iterations per chain | 10,000 | 250,000 |
| Checkpoints per chain | 20 | 1,000 |
| Retained draws per chain | 100 | 500 |
| Global control | 134.9 MB | 98.0 MB |
| Chain control | about 224 KB | about 1.14 MB |
| Chunk files, all chains | 40 | 4,000 |
| Allocated cache size | 1.89 GB (1.76 GiB) | 17.89 GB (16.66 GiB) |

The SHIELD run used 500-iteration checkpoints, burned 5,000 iterations, and
thinned by 50. Each chain recorded 9.4–9.7 hours, so a checkpoint took about 28–29
minutes. A representative post-burn chunk was 44,190,434 bytes and held ten draws.
A compressed sidecar containing its samples, likelihoods, acceptance counts, chain
and iteration metadata was 5,049 bytes—about 8,750 times smaller. Loading the full
chunk from local temporary storage took about one second. Copying a different 44.2
MB chunk through one VPN-mounted-share measurement took 105 seconds; that timing
describes the measurement path, not server-local throughput.

The EHE cache had no burn, 250-iteration checkpoints, and thinning by 500. It
therefore wrote alternating empty and one-draw MCMC chunks: an inspected empty
chunk was 1.14 MB, while a one-draw chunk was 7.74 MB. The corresponding diagnostic
payload was 6.7 KB. This confirms that the large serialization cost comes from
captured model/simulation state and fixed object structure, not the parameter table
needed for mixing checks.

Both caches used the older chain-control schema without per-chunk seeds. The cache
format carries neither a schema version nor a package ref. The compatible package
commit available in the repository history is `bayesian.simulations@1da1851`; the
per-chunk seed schema was added later in `b170ce7`. The serialized objects alone do
not identify the exact server installation, but they establish that the newer
schema was not used for these runs.

This is not transparently forward-compatible. Loading an inspected old control
after loading the current `bayesian.simulations@4e0d13e` class definition succeeds
only as an invalid S4 object: `validObject()` reports the missing `seeds` slot, and
accessing that slot fails. The current resume loop requires `chain.control@seeds`.
Upgrading the package can therefore strand an incomplete pre-seed cache unless an
explicit compatibility or migration path is provided. A migration cannot recreate
the random stream that the old cache never recorded; at most it can record new
future seeds and disclose that boundary.

## Architecture options

### 1. JHEEM-only cache reader

Expand `jheem2::get.calibration.progress()` or add application utilities that load
the serialized controls and chunks directly.

**Advantages:** smallest apparent diff; immediately understands JHEEM's
version/location/calibration directory convention.

**Costs:** duplicates knowledge of private support-package classes, leaves the
exported support-package interface unfinished, and couples every observer to an
unversioned serialization layout. It also cannot solve job state without analysis
or scheduler context.

**Assessment:** useful as a disposable prototype, not the durable boundary.

### 2. Support-package snapshot plus analysis-layer policy and report — recommended

Add a defensive `inspect.mcmc.cache()` API to `bayesian.simulations`. It returns
plain, schema-versioned status data across old and new chain controls. When a chunk
finishes, publish its small parameter/likelihood/acceptance payload atomically from
the in-memory MCMC object. Add a checkpoint hook that can consume a common prefix
of those sidecars and publish a structured stop request. Add the diagnostic policy
and a separate command in `jheem_analyses` that discovers JHEEM calibration
directories, supplies location/application context, and renders the snapshot and
decisions for operators. Full science-chunk reads remain an explicit legacy
fallback, not the routine online path.

**Advantages:** the package that owns the cache owns its read contract; the
analysis layer owns workflow discovery and presentation; other applications can
reuse the inspector. The status path reads only per-chain controls, while the
diagnostic path avoids repeatedly deserializing gigabytes of simulation state.

**Costs:** requires a bounded write-path change, coordinated changes in two
repositories, backward-compatible handling of the pre-seed schema, and a supported
way to install a matching `bayesian.simulations` version. Job state still needs
optional process integration or an explicit run manifest.

**Assessment:** best balance of immediate utility and a boundary that can survive
the next cache-format change. It supports the requested early-stop behavior
without pretending that a chain-local parameter table contains cross-chain state.

### 3. Structured run-event sidecar

Instrument launchers and the sampler to publish a format-versioned manifest,
heartbeat, checkpoint events, and terminal success/failure records atomically. A
monitor consumes those small files and loads MCMC chunks only on demand.

**Advantages:** distinguishes queued/running/stale/failed/completed states, records
code and environment identity, and avoids polling large serialized science
objects.

**Costs:** changes the run path, requires regression coverage and migration rules,
and must accommodate both Slurm and server-launched processes plus the custom Ryan
White workflow.

**Assessment:** likely destination, but unnecessary for proving the first operator
value.

## Recommended first slice

### Support-package contract

Implement a status-only `inspect.mcmc.cache(dir)` in `bayesian.simulations` that:

- copies each chain-control file to a temporary path before loading it;
- retries transient copy/load failures with a bounded backoff;
- validates the agreement of cache IDs across readable chains, dimensions, and
  referenced completed chunks, while reporting timestamp and metadata anomalies;
- recognizes the observed pre-seed and current chain-control schemas without
  silently upgrading either;
- returns plain data rather than serialized S4 objects;
- reports per chain: completed/total chunks, whether retained sampling has begun,
  cumulative acceptance, completed runtime, chunk-based estimated remaining time,
  last checkpoint time, completeness, and a `readable`/`unknown` status;
- labels checkpoint freshness without claiming that stale means failed; and
- versions the returned snapshot schema. A cache-format version belongs in a later
  writer change.

The default status path should not load the global control or MCMC chunks or parse
human-readable logs. A representative global control was 134.9 MB and took 9.8
seconds merely to deserialize from local temporary storage, while chain controls
were about 224 KB. Exact iteration counts and configuration can be cached at setup
in the new small manifest rather than repeatedly loading the global control.

### Checkpoint-policy contract

At each post-burn checkpoint, extract samples, likelihoods, acceptance counts,
chain, and iteration metadata from the in-memory MCMC object and publish a
chunk-specific, schema-versioned sidecar using temporary-file-plus-rename. Define
a narrow hook in `bayesian.simulations` that runs only after the science chunk,
diagnostic sidecar, and chain control have been durably published. Its input is a
plain snapshot over the common available sidecar prefix plus immutable context;
its output is a validated decision. Use another small atomic sidecar for diagnostic
results and stop requests rather than changing the meaning of `chunk.done`.

Pass the hook at run time rather than serializing an application closure into the
already large global control. The no-hook path must produce the same science cache
and MCMC results as before. Legacy caches can be inspected for status and analyzed
offline by loading full chunks, but they cannot gain the efficient online path
retroactively. Resume of an incomplete pre-seed cache must use its compatible
package or an explicit, provenance-recorded migration; the new code must not
fabricate compatibility silently.

For the first policy, agree on and name exactly one diagnostic. Configure its
minimum post-burn draws per chain, evaluation cadence, threshold, and number or
fraction of flagged parameters required to stop, including whether the condition
must persist or fail to improve across checks. Save the flagged parameter names,
values, and recent diagnostic history. Do not label a threshold crossing
“non-mixing” or “hopeless” unless the chosen diagnostic supports that
interpretation.

### Operator command

Add a thin command in `jheem_analyses` that accepts a root, version, calibration
code, and locations; discovers the standard JHEEM cache directories; calls the
support-package inspector; and prints a location-by-chain table. A machine-readable
JSON or CSV mode makes the same contract usable by a future web view without
choosing a dashboard framework now.

Its states should be deliberately conservative: `not set up`, `checkpointing`,
`complete`, `unreadable/unknown`, and `no recent checkpoint`. `running`, `queued`,
and `failed` require corroborating process/scheduler or manifest evidence.

### Validation gate

Before calling the slice complete:

1. Test synthetic caches before setup, during burn, after one and multiple chunks,
   with uneven chains, complete, resumed, deleted, and deliberately truncated
   controls.
2. Verify that the inspector never writes inside the observed calibration tree.
3. Run repeated status reads against a live test calibration while it checkpoints;
   transient states must become `unknown`, not crash or report corruption.
4. Verify both observed cache schemas, including inconsistent metadata and a
   deliberately truncated control, without rewriting legacy artifacts. Test
   current-source loading and the explicit refusal or migration behavior for an
   incomplete pre-seed cache.
5. Prove byte-for-byte or field-level equivalence of the science outputs with no
   hook configured, and deterministic policy decisions over fixed sidecar fixtures.
6. Shadow a live server calibration without permission to stop it; measure
   checkpoint publication, sidecar overhead, server-local read time, concurrent
   chains, and recovery after an interrupted write.
7. Confirm output and stop behavior against the normal shared-server workflow;
   verify the Rockfish path separately if it remains supported.

### Follow-on diagnostics

After the first policy proves safe and cheap, use the parameter sidecars for
additional parameter and total-log-likelihood traces, windowed acceptance, split
rank-normalized R-hat, and bulk/tail ESS. Diagnostics should state when there are
too few chains or draws to interpret. Full-chunk loading remains available for
offline legacy analysis, not routine polling. Piecewise likelihood behavior is not
stored in the current chunks and would require either recomputation from retained
simulations or new instrumentation.

Structured run manifests, scheduler linkage, sub-checkpoint callbacks, and custom
Ryan White status are separate increments.

## Open questions

- On the shared servers, is each chain always a separate operating-system job, or
  are some active workflows multi-chain parent processes? What scope should an
  early stop have: one chain, all chains for one location, or a larger run?
- Which upcoming calibration can be observed in shadow mode, and which exact
  launcher, package library, server-local cache path, and process layout will it
  use?
- How long can a healthy chunk run for each active calibration before a freshness
  warning becomes useful?
- Do operators primarily need location/chain completion, likelihood behavior,
  failure notification, or all three in that order?
- Which calculation does “mixing statistic” mean for this feature? What minimum
  post-burn sample size, cadence, threshold, and flagged-parameter count are
  scientifically defensible?
- Should a policy-hook error allow sampling to continue while recording the error,
  or fail the calibration? Who may resume or override a policy stop?
- Can `bayesian.simulations` be pinned and upgraded reproducibly on the shared
  servers? Which cache migration or compatibility policy is required for the
  observed pre-seed schema?
- Which process identifiers and terminal states can the server launchers publish?
  Should the alternative Rockfish path record scheduler IDs or query Slurm
  separately?
- Is the custom Ryan White fitting path part of the requested calibration feature?

## Durable home and exit condition

This page remains the cross-repository investigation record while the proposal is
being evaluated. If adopted:

- the cache schema, inspector API, atomicity guarantees, and package tests belong
  in `bayesian.simulations`;
- the command, scheduler integration, and operator runbook belong in
  `jheem_analyses`; and
- this wiki retains only the cross-repository execution map, supported workflow,
  and decision rationale.

The investigation graduates when the supported status path is documented in those
repositories and its cross-repository contract is recorded here. It should instead
be retired if a different architecture is selected or the relevant calibration
workflow is replaced.
